name: Illusory Truth Effect
description: Repeated statements feel truer than new ones, even when repetition adds no new evidence. Familiarity can be misread as credibility.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in onboarding copy, marketing claims, political or trust-and-safety contexts, and any product that repeats messages often enough that fluency gets mistaken for truth.
prevalence_note: Used in content-design, persuasion, trust-and-safety, and misinformation-adjacent product work, but not usually treated as a baseline interaction-design law in mainstream UX teaching.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of 51 studies confirmed the repetition-induced truth effect is real and reliable, at a medium effect size — larger when comparing repeated statements against genuinely new ones than when comparing the same statement's rating across two encounters — consistent with a 'processing fluency' account: the felt ease of processing a familiar statement gets misread as a signal that it's true.
findings.effect_size: d ≈ 0.39 (within-items) / d ≈ 0.50 (between-items) — per secondary characterization, see this source's verification_note
findings.effect_size_ci: reported elsewhere as 95% CI [0.30, 0.49] within-items, [0.43, 0.57] between-items — same caveat as effect_size
findings.source_title: The Truth About the Truth: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Truth Effect

findings.description: Statements repeated across three rating sessions (two weeks apart) received significantly higher truth ratings than non-repeated statements — true for both actually-true and actually-false statements — the founding demonstration that mere repetition, independent of accuracy, increases how true a claim feels.
findings.source_title: Frequency and the Conference of Referential Validity
findings.source_venue: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
